abstract: Significance Cannabinoid type 1 receptors (CB1Rs) are targets for endocannabinoids and cannabis in the brain and trigger the brain’s reward circuitry. However, it remains elusive how CB1Rs acting as Gi/o-coupled receptors modulate neurotransmitter release in a retrograde manner. Here, we show that an epilepsy-associated protein, the alpha subunit of Go, Gαo, is the key protein transmitting CB1R signaling at presynaptic terminals. We find that Gαo interacts with CB1Rs and multiple cerebellar synaptic proteins essential for neurotransmitter release. A targeted deletion of presynaptic Gαo causes dysregulation of cerebellar excitability and synaptic plasticity, mirroring the phenotypes found in CB1R knockout (KO) animals. These findings offer unique insights into how Go contributes to the suppression of epileptic seizures and the retrograde regulation of neurotransmission.

body:
G proteins transmit extracellular signals from hormones and neurotransmitters to intracellular responses via G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). Ligand binding to a GPCR triggers dissociation of Gα from Gβγ dimers, each initiating downstream signaling cascades through various effector molecules. While G proteins share Gβγ, the specificity is determined by Gα. Understanding the interplay between GPCRs and G proteins is crucial for deciphering cellular signaling complexities and identifying potential therapeutic targets for diverse diseases.
GNAO1
encodes the alpha subunit of Go proteins (Gαo) and is associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 17 (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man: 615473) (
1
–
6
). Go is the most abundant G protein at synapses, comprising up to 0.5% of brain membrane proteins (
7
–
10
). Despite its prevalence, the role of Go remains relatively unknown compared to other G proteins due to practical hurdles for loss-of-function studies. Mutations of
Gnao1
induce early infant mortality in mouse models (
2
,
11
,
12
), mirroring symptoms observed in patients with DEE (
1
–
6
). However, it remains unclear how the lack of proper functions of Go leads to DEE.
The cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) is a Gi/o-coupled receptor predominantly found in the brain (
13
,
14
), serving as a receptor for endocannabinoids (eCBs) as well as CBs derived from the medicinal plant
Cannabis sativa
(marijuana) in the brain. Due to their hydrophobicity, eCBs activate CB1Rs in synaptic terminals (
15
). CB1R activation induces suppression of neurotransmitter release from synaptic terminals, attenuating afferent presynaptic inputs (
15
). However, the molecular mechanisms for CB1R-mediated inhibition of neurotransmitter release remain elusive because most studies have focused on the Gi aspect, despite Go being more prevalent than Gi and highly activated by the CB1R agonist, WIN55,212 in the brain (
16
,
17
). This inference arises because there is currently no direct method available to measure Gαo activity (
18
,
19
), whereas the Gαi activity can be measured through adenylyl cyclase inhibition and the subsequent cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) reduction.
In this study, we implemented two strategies to investigate the interactions between CB1R and Go in vivo and in vitro. First, we conducted proteomic analyses to identify Go-interacting proteins within synaptosomal fractions of the brain and then examined the downstream signaling pathway of Go. Second, we developed a non-DEE mouse model by selectively deleting the
Gnao1
gene in the proliferating progenitors of granule cell neurons (GCNs) in the cerebellum and then evaluated the CB1R-dependent synaptic plasticity. These approaches allowed a detailed investigation into mechanistic aspects and functional implications of Go in regulating synaptic plasticity and motor learning via CB1R. Our findings suggest that disturbing this regulation by the deletion of
Gnao1
within the cerebellum could impair motor function while such disruption across the entire brain might lead to DEE, as evidenced in global knockout (KO) mice or DEE patients.
Results
Interaction of CB1R with Gi/o Proteins in the Cerebellar Membrane.
To investigate the interaction of Go with CB1R, cerebellar synaptosomal P2 fractions were solubilized in CHAPS detergent and immunoprecipitated using an anti-CB1R antibody (
Fig. 1
A
). Western blot analysis indicated that CB1R existed as a complex with Gαo and the CB1R::Gαo interaction was disrupted by guanosine 5'-(γ-thio)triphosphate (GTPγS), a nonhydrolyzable G protein activator. In comparison, antagonists/inverse agonists such as AM251 and SR141716 also disrupted these interactions, whereas WIN55,212, a CB1R agonist, had no effect (
Fig. 1
B
and
C
). Likewise, CB1R also interacted with Gαi to a lesser degree, and the interaction was disrupted by GTPγS, AM251, and SR141716, although WIN55,212 slightly increased the CB1R:: Gαi complex formation (
Fig. 1
B
and
C
). The effect of guanosine 5'-triphosphate (GTP) on the CB1R::Go interaction was further analyzed using Glutathione S-transferase (GST) pull-down assays. GST-conjugated inactive Gαo [Gαo-guanosine 5'-diphosphate (GDP)] or active Gαo (Gαo-GTPγS) beads were incubated with solubilized crude synaptosomal P2 fractions of cerebellum (
Fig. 1
D
). CB1R interacted with Gαo-GDP but minimally with Gαo-GTPγS (
Fig. 1
E
). The inactive status of Gαo-GDP was verified by its strong interaction with Gβγ. These results suggest that CB1R prefers interacting with inactive heterotrimeric Go rather than with active free Gαo.

Go-Interacting Proteins in the Brain Synaptosomes.
Because Go lacks enzymatic activity, we used crude synaptosomal P2 fractions to probe for Go-interacting proteins at the synapse to gain further insight into how CB1R signals are transmitted. Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with an anti-Gαo antibody and mass spectrometry analysis revealed 211 proteins to specifically interact with Gαo either directly or indirectly (
Fig. 2
A
and
Dataset S1
). Western blot analyses confirmed the interactions with Go including syntaxin-binding protein 1 (Stxbp1, also known as Munc18-1), synapsin I (Syn1), synaptosome-associated protein 25 (Snap25), synaptobrevin 2 (Vamp2/Syb2), syntaxin 1 (Stx1), the catalytic subunit of PKA (PKA-Cα), and additional proteins such as synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (Sv2a) and synaptotagmin 1 (Syt1) (
Fig. 2
B
). Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) revealed significant enrichment of canonical pathways across various functional categories, particularly those associated with the neurotransmitter release cycle, synaptogenesis signaling pathway, neurotransmitter uptake and metabolism, and synaptic long-term depression and potentiation (
Fig. 2
C
). Further analysis revealed a protein–protein interaction network of Go-associated proteins, including Gls, Rab3a, Slc1a2, Slc1a3, Snap25, Stx1a, Stxbp1, Syn1, Syn2, and Vamp2, which play roles in the release of neurotransmitters, particularly glutamate (highlighted in purple in
Fig. 2
D
), along with dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine at the presynaptic terminals (purple in
SI Appendix
, Fig. S1
). Several proteins involved in synaptogenesis signaling pathways were identified, including Camk2a, Cfl1, Mapk3, Mapt, Nsf, Prkar2b, Rab3a, Snap25, Stx16, Stx1a, Stxbp1, Syn11, Syn2, and Vamp2 (purple in
Fig. 2
E
). These findings suggest a potential role for Go in regulating synapse formation and neurotransmitter release.

Cerebellum-Specific Deletion of
Gnao1
.
In situ hybridization revealed that
Gnao1
mRNA was expressed in most cells of the cerebellar cortex, including Purkinje cells (PCs), GCNs, and interneurons of the molecular layer (ML).
Gnao1
mRNA was detected in the perikaryons of calbindin-positive PCs (
SI Appendix

A–C
). Tamoxifen administration during postnatal days 4 to 7 (P4-7) in
Gli1
CreERT2
::R26R
YFP/+
mice (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
D
) induced yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) expression in GCN progenitors in the external granule layer (arrowheads in
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
E1
,
F
, and
G
). Progenitor cells proliferate, migrate inward, and differentiate into GCNs. YFP was also expressed in the glial fibrillary acidic protein glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-positive Bergmann glia (BG) cells (arrows in
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
G1
). Importantly, YFP expression was absent in Purkinje cell protein 2 (Pcp2)-positive PCs (asterisks in
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
F
and
G
), parvalbumin-positive interneurons, and the inferior olivary nucleus (IONs) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
H
and
I
). The data indicated that
Gli1
could selectively delete the
Gnao1
gene in GCNs and BGs among all Gαo-expressing cells (
SI Appendix

).
However, tamoxifen administration starting at P4 was not sufficient to fully deplete the remarkably stable Gαo protein in the presence of two
floxed
alleles of
Gnao1
f/f
mice (
Fig. 3
D

Δ/−

Gli1

Fig. 3

–
C

20

Δ

loxP

−

Gnao
1 cKO (
Fig. 3
B
) (
12
,
21
). Depletion of stable Gαo protein in the
Gnao1
cKO cerebellum was confirmed through western blot analysis using anti-Gαo. The decrease in the total level of all Gα subtypes detected by the pan-Gα antibody reflected the relative abundance of Gαo compared to other G-protein types, as the expression levels of Gαi, Gαq, and Gαs/olf remained unaltered (
Fig. 3
E
and
F
). It should be noted that the reduction in Gαo levels was accompanied by a decrease in Gβγ levels. Within the superficial ML where the GCN axons establish parallel fibers (PFs), the Gαo-immunoreactivity was reduced compared to the deep ML (
Fig. 3
G
–
I
). Collectively, these findings suggest effective depletion of Gαo in the presynaptic fibers originating from GCNs (
Fig. 3
C
). The cKO mice displayed no gross anatomical differences in brain size, cerebellar cytoarchitecture, number of Pcp2-positive PCs, or GCN density compared with their WT littermates (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
). These data indicate that GCN-specific
Gnao1
deletion during the early postnatal period does not significantly impact the overall cerebellar development in contrast to global
Gnao1
KO mice (
22
).

Altered Synaptic Transmission in
Gnao1
cKO Mice.
Since IPA indicated the potential role of Go in synaptogenesis, we assessed the synaptic structures in the cerebellar cortex of
Gnao1
cKO mice. Quantitative analysis of electron microscopic images revealed that the number of synapses was significantly reduced in the superficial ML where Gαo-immunoreactivity was reduced (
Fig. 3
G
–
I
) but not in the deep ML of
Gnao1
cKO (
Fig. 4
A
and
B
). Electrophysiological analysis showed that spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) on PCs increased with higher frequencies and amplitudes in the cKO mice than in the controls (
Fig. 4
C
–
E
). Interestingly, depolarization-induced suppression of excitation (DSE), a hallmark of CB1R-mediated retrograde suppression of transmitter release from GCN fibers, was reduced in
Gnao1
cKO mice (
Fig. 4
G
). These results suggest that
Gnao1
in presynaptic GCNs is essential for CB1R-mediated control of PC excitability.

Ataxia-Like Phenotypes in
Gnao1
cKO Mice.
As expected,
Gnao1
cKO mice exhibited no signs of DEE-like phenotypes and displayed survival rates comparable to those of their WT littermates, thus facilitating behavioral studies. These mice showed normal locomotor activity in the open-field test (
Fig. 5
B
) and eye movements without nystagmus (
Fig. 5
C
), which is a typical cerebellar defect associated with the flocculonodular lobe. However, they exhibited motor deficits in the four-limb hanging wire test, with only 29% of
Gnao1
cKO mice remaining on the inverted screen for 600 s, compared to 82% of controls (
Fig. 5
D
). Given the comparable body weights of the two genotypes (
Fig. 5
A
), the reduced suspension time on the grid may suggest decreased muscle/grip strength in
Gnao1
cKO mice rather than decreased muscle mass. Footprint analysis revealed a 5 to 10% decrease in the stride and stance lengths for both the forelimbs and hindlimbs of
Gnao1
cKO mice, whereas sway length remained unchanged for the hindlimbs and slightly decreased for the forelimbs (
Fig. 5
E
and
F
). Additionally,
Gnao1
cKO mice showed increased foot fault errors in the beam balance tests, with no changes in the traverse time on the beam (
Fig. 5
G
). Higher foot fault errors and altered footprint patterns suggest cerebellar gait defects that indicate mild ataxia. In the rotarod test at constant speeds below 15 rpm,
Gnao1
cKO mice performed comparably to controls but exhibited difficulty at speeds exceeding 25 rpm (
Fig. 5
H
). Motor learning ability was evaluated using an accelerating speed ranging from 4 to 40 rpm. Control mice initially faced challenges but gradually adapted over five trial sessions (
Fig. 5
I
). In contrast,
Gnao1
cKO mice encountered difficulties from the first day and consistently struggled throughout the five trial days, showing no improvement (
Fig. 5
I
). Taken together, GCN-specific deletion of
Gnao1
impairs motor coordination and learning, resulting in a mild ataxic phenotype. These findings underscore the crucial role of presynaptic Gαo protein in cerebellum-related motor function.

Discussion
Previous studies on the physiological roles of Go have been hampered by a perinatal mortality of global KO animals (
12
). Using seizure-free cKO mice with targeted deletion of
Gnao1
in the cerebellum, the present study revealed unique functions of Go in the brain regarding neural network architecture and synaptic plasticity.
The specific deletion of
Gnao1
in presynaptic GCNs was achieved by
Gli1
-mediated Cre recombinase expression in GCN progenitors (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
). The stable Gαo proteins synthesized before tamoxifen treatment are gradually reduced as the progenitor cells proliferate and differentiate into GCNs. The Gαo deficiency in presynaptic GCNs is verified by the decreased Gαo immunoreactivity in the superficial ML but not in deep ML (
Fig. 3
G
–
I
). In the superficial ML, distal dendrites of PCs receive input mainly from PFs of GCNs, whereas primary dendrites in the deep ML receive inputs from climbing fibers (CFs) of ION neurons (
23
–
25
). Accordingly, synaptic connections with PCs were notably reduced in the superficial ML but not in the deep ML (
Fig. 4
A
and
B
). Taken together, these results suggest a role for Go in synapse formation, which is consistent with the IPA enrichment pathway analysis (
Fig. 2
C
and
E
).
Importantly,
Gnao1
cKO mice exhibited reduced DSE (
Fig. 4
G
), a form of short-term synaptic plasticity involved in glutamatergic transmission. DSE occurs when eCBs released from depolarized postsynaptic PCs bind to CB1R receptors located at the presynaptic terminal, resulting in the retrograde inhibition of glutamate release from the presynaptic GCN (
26
,
27
). By dampening excitatory synaptic transmission, DSE counteracts the excessive excitation of postsynaptic neurons, thereby contributing to the overall balance and homeostasis of neuronal activity in the brain (
Fig. 6
B
). In the absence of Go, this CB1R-mediated retrograde feedback is disrupted, resulting in a decrease in DSE (
Fig. 6
C
). Concurrently, there is an increase in sEPSC, despite a decrease in synapse number (
Fig. 4
). The increased excitability could result from impaired CB1R signaling, which normally suppresses intrinsic excitability and reduces the frequency of sEPSCs or sIPSCs (
28
). Alternatively, this could be due to changes in synaptic vesicle release probability in the absence of Go, as Go interacts with the SNARE complex (
Fig. 2
). Further studies are needed to elucidate the precise mechanisms by which Go regulates synaptic transmission at presynaptic terminals.
Fig. 6.
A schematic diagram illustrating the interaction between CB1Rs and Go proteins at the synapse. (
A
) eCBs binding to CB1R activates heterotrimeric Go, leading to the dissociation of Gαo and Gβ. Go interacts with a variety of proteins involved in neurotransmitter release, including PKA, Syn1, Syt1, Stxbp1, Snap25, Vamp2, and Sv2a. (
B
) In the WT mice, eCBs released from depolarized postsynaptic PCs bind to CB1R in the presynaptic GCN terminals. Activated CB1R retrogradely inhibits the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles, evoking DSE in PCs. (
C
) In
Gnao1
cKO mice, CB1R-mediated regulation of neurotransmitter release is disrupted, resulting in reduced DSE along with enhanced sEPSCs.
The presynaptic role of Gi/o has been demonstrated in association with CB1R. Overexpression of pertussis toxin-insensitive Gαo1 and Gαi2/3 can rescue the CB1R-mediated inhibition of EPSCs in autaptic hippocampal neurons (
29
). Compared to those studies, our loss-of-function study provides direct evidence of Gαo’s involvement in CB1R-mediated synaptic neurotransmission within a more native physiological system.
Previous studies involving either global or GCN-specific deletion of the gene encoding CB1R have demonstrated DSE disruption (
14
,
30
,
31
). The absence of this negative feedback control in the cerebellum manifests as impaired motor coordination and learning ability, resulting in a mild ataxia phenotype (
Fig. 5
D
–
I
), whereas its absence throughout the brain can lead to a DEE-like phenotype, as observed in the global KO mouse model (
12
). Our findings indicate an interaction between Go and CB1R, along with the disrupted synaptic plasticity observed in
Gnao1
cKO and CB1R KO mice, strongly suggesting that Go is the primary G protein mediating CB1R-dependent retrograde regulation of synaptic transmission in the cerebellum. However, in
Gnao1
cKO mice, eye movement remained normal without nystagmus, a well-known indicator of cerebellar abnormalities affecting the vestibulo-ocular reflex (
32
) (
Fig. 5
C
). It can be ascribed to the significant amount of Gαo protein remaining in the flocculus and paraflocculus in the lobule X, as indicated by the low expression of a reporter gene in this area (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
J
).
Similar studies in knock-in mice carrying a human
GNAO1
variant mutation showed that spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic current was reduced without changes in sEPSC. This mutation resulted in the aberrant splicing and premature termination of protein synthesis, leading to haploinsufficiency of Gαo protein with increased free Gβγ (
33
). In comparison, the Gαo depletion in our cKO mice resulted in a concomitant decrease in Gβγ levels (
Fig. 3
E
). Further studies are needed to determine whether the different results regarding sEPSCs are due to increased vs. unaltered free Gβγ levels. Alternatively, the differences might be related to
Gnao1
monoallelic deletion in both presynaptic neurons and postsynaptic PCs vs. an additional biallelic deletion (
−/Δ
) in presynaptic GCNs.
It has been shown that Gβγ released from heterotrimeric Gi/o proteins can inhibit exocytosis of synaptic vesicles by interacting with SNARE proteins, activating G-protein-gated inwardly rectifying K
+
channels, or inhibiting voltage-gated Ca
2+
channels (
34
,
35
). It is conceivable that Gαo acts as a scaffold to anchor Gβγ at the synapse, and the concomitant reduction of the Gβγ reservoir may decrease the effectiveness of retrograde inhibition, resulting in increased sEPSCs in
Gnao1
cKO mice (
Fig. 4
C
–
E
). Alternatively, Go may play a distinct role in the modulation of short-term plasticity. Previous studies, including our own, have demonstrated that Gαo interacts with various proteins including APP (
36
), Snap25 (
37
), Vamp2 (
38
), Rab4/5 (
39
), voltage-dependent Ca
2+
channels (
40
), Pcp2 (L7) (
41
), Psd95 (
42
), Src kinase (
43
), and PKA (
44
,
45
). We also have shown that Gαo acts as a scaffold for PKA without affecting its kinase activity (
44
). Of particular interest is the interaction between Gαo and Sv2a, a binding target of the widely used anticonvulsant drug, levetiracetam (Keppra®) (
46
) (
Fig. 2
B
). It should be noted that CB1R is not present in the proteomics data (
Fig. 2
D
and
E
). This absence can be attributed to CB1R’s resistance to Triton X100, requiring the use of stronger detergent like CHAPS for solubilization (
Fig. 1
A
). Although our study demonstrated the interaction of Gαo with multiple presynaptic proteins, it remains unclear whether these interactions are direct or indirect (
47
). Further studies are needed to elucidate how Gαo interact with diverse proteins to modulate the CB1R signals in the neurons.
In humans,
GNAO1
-related disorders are often caused by de novo pathogenic variants, encompassing a broad spectrum of conditions, including epilepsy and hyperkinetic movement disorders (
6
,
48
). Knock-in mice carrying human
GNAO1
variant mutations exhibit similar patterns to those observed in human patients, confirming its autosomal dominant inheritance (
6
,
33
,
48
). The
Gnao1
cKO mice used in this study differ from the human disease in that monoallelic deletions do not induce abnormal phenotypes in heterozygotes (
+/−
), while biallelic deletions (−/−) result in DEE-like phenotypes and early lethality, suggesting an autosomal recessive inheritance in mice (
11
,
12
).
The limitation of this study is that
Gli1
CreERT2
induces recombination in BG cells (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
G
) (
20
). BG cells play an essential role in cerebellar cortical development, and their impairment may be responsible for non-cell-autonomous neuronal degeneration in distinct forms of ataxia (
49
). However, in
Gnao1
cKO mice, the cytoarchitecture, including the thickness of the ML and GCL (presynaptic) and the number of PCs (postsynaptic), appeared similar to those in WT littermates (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
), suggesting that the function of Go in BG cells may be minimal.
Gi/o-coupled GPCRs encompass receptors for various neurotransmitters and hormones, including acetylcholine, adenosine, adrenaline, CBs, chemokines, dopamine, GABA, glutamate, histamine, melatonin, opioids, prostaglandins, serotonin, and somatostatin (
50
,
51
). Historically, these ligands have been shown to exert their physiological effects by activating Gi, leading to a decrease in intracellular cAMP levels and the subsequent attenuation of PKA-dependent signaling (
52
). This study is the first to demonstrate that Go, a key Gi/o-coupled to CB1R, plays a pivotal role in neurotransmitter release and synaptogenesis signaling pathways at the presynaptic terminal in the cerebellum. Notably, numerous psychoactive substances, including caffeine, nicotine, marijuana, specific pain modulators, and certain antidepressants, exert their effects via direct and indirect interactions with Gi/o-coupled GPCRs. We anticipate that our findings will provide valuable insights into other Gi/o-coupled GPCRs from the perspective of the Go-dependent pathway.
